title: L2-Bench: An Evaluation Benchmark for Measuring LLM Capabilities in Second Language Education
claim: Relative strengths and weaknesses across task categories differ from overall ranking, with structured tasks easier than open-ended ones.
layout: single heatmap, models as rows, competencies as columns, rank colorbar at right
description: A single large heatmap titled 'Model Performance by Competency (cell = score %, colour = rank)'. Rows are nine LLMs, ordered roughly best to worst, from Opus 4.7 and GPT 5.4 down to Qwen3 32B and Magistral Small. Columns are twelve numbered competencies, such as Course Planning, Lesson Planning, Exchange Partner, Giving Feedback and Professional Development. Their labels are rotated 45 degrees. Each cell shows a score percentage. Cell colour shows the model's rank within that competency, on a red-to-green diverging scale. Dark green means rank 1 and dark red means rank 9. A vertical colorbar on the right labels the scale 'Rank within competency (1 = best)'. The eye goes first to the green top rows and the red bottom rows. Column-wise variation shows that rank differs by competency, and the lowest scores fall in open-ended columns.
caption: Model performance by competency. Relative strengths and weaknesses are legible independently of a model's overall level. All models perform relatively well on structured output tasks (lesson and activity planning) but less well on open-ended competencies (conversational exchange partner, giving feedback, evaluating performance).
abstract: Despite rapid AI adoption in education, rigorous evaluation of AI-powered educational (AIED) systems remains critically underdeveloped, particularly in second language (L2) education, one of the most common yet least evaluated AI applications. We introduce L2-Bench, an open-source benchmark of 1,000+ task-response pairs to aid the pedagogy-led evaluation of LLM capabilities relating to language learning and assessment. Crucially, L2-Bench measures model performativity on the application of learning experience design principles rather than mere knowledge of those principles or broad learning outcomes. Our contributions include: (1) a validated taxonomy of 12 competencies and 31 subcompetencies validated by 200+ expert practitioners (task authenticity: 4.42/5.00, criteria adequacy: 4.18/5.00); (2) a rubric-based evaluation methodology that we believe can, if adapted, generalize to similar (open-ended, qualitative) disciplines; (3) an evaluation dataset that produces reliable signal about model strengths, weaknesses, and contextual robustness across diverse L2 education scenarios. We find that, among large models, Claude Opus 4.7 performs best overall (85.5%), though is marginally outperformed on several constituent tasks. We also find that performance drops notably on harder tasks (69.9% to 73.4%). L2-Bench provides education stakeholders better methods to make more informed decisions about real-world AIED adoption, use, and governance, while advancing the maturing science of AI evaluations for education.
